concepts.title: Central Tendency: The Idea of an Average
concepts.definition: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents a whole data set -- an average around which the observations cluster. The chapter presents the three classic measures: arithmetic mean, median and mode, each suited to different kinds of data and purposes.
concepts.key_idea: One number to stand for many -- the average condenses a series into its centre.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest105.txt central tendency sections (measures of central tendency, arithmetic mean median mode, criteria of a good average)

solution_steps.explain: An average condenses scattered observations into one representative figure.
Arithmetic mean uses all values, median uses position, mode uses frequency.
Data type and purpose decide which measure represents the centre best.

concepts.title: Arithmetic Mean: Simple and Weighted
concepts.definition: The arithmetic mean divides the sum of all observations by their number; for a frequency series, values are first multiplied by their frequencies. A weighted mean multiplies each value by an assigned importance before averaging, letting significance -- not just occurrence -- shape the result.
concepts.key_idea: Sum over count -- the mean uses every observation, which is its strength and its sensitivity alike.

concepts.title: Median and Mode: Position and Frequency
concepts.definition: The median is the middle observation of an ordered series -- the value splitting the data in equal halves -- and for an even count it is the average of the two central values. The mode is the most frequently occurring value. Both resist extreme values, which distort the mean.
concepts.key_idea: Median sits at the middle of the queue; mode is the crowd's favourite -- both laugh at extremes.
